Pele Yoetz 62:42: Scoffing - namely, those occupied with jesting, or one who mocks his fellow to increase laughter and joy - their evil is great, and our Rabbis, of blessed memory, already said (Avodah Zarah 18b) that scoffing begins in affliction and ends in destruction, may the Merciful One save us.
Pele Yoetz 62:43: Falsehood is a severe sin, like worshiping idols - only for the sake of peace is it permitted to alter the truth, and there is even a mitzvah to lie if it cannot otherwise suffice. And likewise there are matters that the Sages themselves would alter, such as regarding modesty and not revealing one's own praise (Bava Metzia 23b), in the manner of what they said (Berachot 4a): teach your tongue to say "I do not know." And any similar case - whoever lies for the sake of Heaven is permitted, and they have already said (Horayot 10b): great is a transgression performed for its own [proper] sake.
Pele Yoetz 62:44: Whoever curses his fellow, or himself, or one to whom he is obligated in honor, or even if he curses one who is [merely] obligated to honor him - a causeless curse shall come upon him, and even if it is not causeless, the curse divides between them: if his curse is not fulfilled, it deducts from his own merit; and if it is fulfilled, it is counted as bloodshed for that man, and he shall be punished for having caused evil, besides his punishment for having transgressed the word of the Merciful One. And especially one who excommunicates his fellow or calls him accursed, which involves a form of excommunication or a ban, and thereby falls into the category of one who excommunicates someone not liable to excommunication - for one who excommunicates [unjustly] is himself put under a ban, God forbid.
Pele Yoetz 62:45: Whoever speaks to his father or mother harshly, brazenly, in a manner of disgrace and anger, falls into the category of "cursed is he who dishonors his father and mother" (Deuteronomy 27:16). And likewise one who speaks harshly to an orphan or a widow transgresses "you shall not afflict any widow or orphan" (Exodus 22:21). And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, already said (Shabbat 11a - referring to the annulment of decree, adapted): under Ishmael, but not under [causing distress to] orphans and widows. And even the teacher who teaches Torah to orphans must have mercy on them and guide them and discipline them calmly and with compassion.
Pele Yoetz 62:46: Whoever gives his fellow a bad nickname, even if it has become common usage, and whoever shames his fellow's face in public, has no share in the World to Come (Bava Metzia 58b).
Pele Yoetz 62:47: "You shall not answer in a dispute" (Exodus 23:2) - for the one who answers holds fast to the dispute and causes it to be fruitful and multiply until the flame rises. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, already said (Chullin 89a): "He hangs the earth upon nothing [belimah]" (Job 26:7) - upon one who restrains [bolem] his mouth at a time of quarrel. And if he does answer, let it be a soft answer that turns away wrath.
Pele Yoetz 62:48: Whoever gives his fellow improper advice transgresses "and before the blind you shall not place a stumbling block" (Leviticus 19:14), and the LORD tests hearts - therefore it is said (ibid.), "and you shall fear your God."
Pele Yoetz 62:49: Whoever steals his fellow's mind, striving through spoken words to know his fellow's secrets, transgresses "you shall not go about as a talebearer" (Leviticus 19:16), as we have written in its place in the name of the "Halachot Ketanot" (part 1, 215) - and even a gentile's mind may not be deceived. And this is permitted to a father, a teacher, and a judge, to steal the heart in order to guide him in the straight way and to bring out a true judgment in its truth.
Pele Yoetz 62:50: The Torah warned that a litigant should not present his own claims to the judge [outside of court proceedings], and also that the judge should not listen to the words of one litigant until his fellow litigant has come. And there is also a warning to the judge not to be gentle to one and harsh to another, and not to favor the poor nor honor the great, but rather treat both equally when they stand before him (Sanhedrin 7:8[Mishnah, Sanhedrin 3:5, cf. Leviticus 19:15]).
Pele Yoetz 62:51: Whoever vows is as though he had built a high place [of forbidden worship], and is called a sinner (Nedarim 22a), as it is written (Deuteronomy 23:23), "but if you refrain from vowing, it shall not be a sin in you." And there are places where the custom is that whoever wishes to go and dwell honorably in the Land of Israel makes a vow to go to the Land of Israel - and this custom is not good, to precede a transgression to a mitzvah; rather, let him go without a vow.
Pele Yoetz 62:52: It is forbidden to mention the name of an idol as the idolaters call it, but rather one must refer to it by a derogatory name. And one who speaks with idolaters stumbles into this if he mentions to them the names of their festival days, which are named after their vanities. And it is good, when one wishes to mention a date, to mention the [secular] month.
Pele Yoetz 62:53: It is forbidden to divine omens - namely, as the common people practice, that when one's piece of bread falls, or when one hiccups (called "sangoroto," and in the German tongue "hitzen"), he says "they are mentioning me." And when there is a spark near the wick of a candle, they say "a guest shall come." And when there is something like a letter-shape at the top of the candle, they say "a letter shall come." Whoever says this and believes in his mind that it is so transgresses "you shall not divine" (Leviticus 19:26). And likewise one who says it is not good to lend or extend credit at the beginning of the week or at the beginning of the day transgresses "you shall not soothsay." Whoever asks sorcerers and diviners to tell him the future transgresses "you shall be blameless with the LORD your God" (Deuteronomy 18:13) (see Pesachim 113b).
Pele Yoetz 62:54: It is forbidden to pervert judgment, as it is said (Leviticus 19:35): "you shall not do injustice in judgment." And this does not apply only to a court case, but to every person with his wife, his children, his servants, and all who are subject to his authority - if they have a sufficient and true claim for not having done his will as he wished, it is not fitting to be angry at them and revile and curse them, as many angry people do. And it is written (Job 31:13): "if I despised the cause of my manservant or my maidservant when they contended with me, what then shall I do when God rises up, and when He visits, what shall I answer Him?"
Pele Yoetz 62:55: It is forbidden to demand a debt from one whom he knows has nothing with which to repay, and it is even forbidden to pass before him, lest he think that he has come to demand it and become frightened.
Pele Yoetz 62:56: It is forbidden to give interest in the form of words - such as greeting first one from whom he has borrowed money, if he was not accustomed to doing so before, or giving him flattering words at the time he repays him. In this too one must be careful, but rather he should say to him, "may you merit [to perform] mitzvot," so that his fellow shall in turn bless him back, as is customary.
Pele Yoetz 62:57: It is forbidden to speak in the synagogue, and especially during prayer and while the Torah scroll is being read. And likewise it is forbidden to speak while listening to Kiddush, Havdalah, the Megillah, the repetition of the Amidah, and all blessings one discharges through hearing, and between the blessing of redemption and the Amidah, and between the blessing over the Hamotzi bread and eating before tasting it, and between washing the hands and eating, and between Mayim Acharonim and Grace after Meals. And it is forbidden to speak between the tefillin of the hand and the tefillin of the head, and even to answer "Kaddish" and "may He be sanctified."
Pele Yoetz 62:58: It is forbidden to speak with women, and especially words of jest, mockery, and levity, which accustom a person toward forbidden relations - and it is even forbidden to greet a woman through her husband, for one does not greet a woman at all; such is the ruling of the Talmud (Kiddushin 70b) and the Shulchan Aruch, not merely a matter of piety.
Pele Yoetz 62:59: It is forbidden for a person to open his mouth to Satan, even if a sharp sword lies upon his neck or he is dangerously ill - let him not despair of mercy (Berachot 10a), but speak good and good shall come. And likewise it is forbidden to speak in the outhouse, for it causes evil to himself.
Pele Yoetz 62:60: It is forbidden to greet a wicked person with peace. And if he is forced to, for the sake of the ways of peace, let him intend that he greets the Name, blessed be He, as it is said (I Samuel 25:6): "and you shall say, 'to life!' and peace be to you [addressed to the LORD, per the interpretation]."
Pele Yoetz 62:61: It is forbidden to speak words of quarrel, and all the more so regarding a quarrel not his own, unless it is to save an oppressed person from his oppressor.
Pele Yoetz 62:62: It is forbidden to speak with pride and contempt or with anger. Let his words always be in a low voice and a gentle tongue, smooth as oil, his palate sweetness itself, and altogether delightful (Song of Songs 5:16).
Pele Yoetz 62:63: It is forbidden to teach an accusation against Israel, and the Holy One, blessed be He, is very exacting about this, for He desires kindness and wants people always to teach a defense for Israel - and words spoken below bear fruit above, whether for good or for less good.
Pele Yoetz 62:64: It is forbidden to put off one's fellow with words, saying to him, "go and come back, and tomorrow I shall give" (Proverbs 3:28), when he has no intention of giving - rather, truth shall guide his way.
Pele Yoetz 62:65: It is forbidden to count Israel [directly, by head] (Yoma 22b).
Pele Yoetz 62:66: It is forbidden to speak of business matters on the Sabbath, and even idle conversation. And in the Yerushalmi (Shabbat 15:3) they said that greeting on the Sabbath was permitted only with difficulty. And in the Holy Zohar (Shemot, page 63) idle words are called a desecration of the Sabbath. And whatever is forbidden to do on the Sabbath is forbidden to discuss doing tomorrow. And telling a gentile [to do prohibited work] is itself a rabbinic prohibition (Shabbat 150a).
Pele Yoetz 62:67: It is forbidden to wrong a Jew with words - namely, to cause distress with words. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Bava Metzia 59a): all gates [of prayer] are locked except the gates of wronging, and it is punished by the Holy One, blessed be He, Himself, since the punishment is more severe - and especially wronging one's wife and the poor and downtrodden, since their tears are readily available, the punishment for wronging them is close at hand, may the Merciful One save us. And many of the common people commit verbal wronging like a madman scattering firebrands, in order to increase laughter and frivolous merriment - may the good Name atone for it.
Pele Yoetz 62:68: It is forbidden to mock the words of the Sages, of blessed memory, and one is punished with boiling excrement (Eruvin 21b). And likewise, one who mocks those who perform important mitzvot is like a harmful bandit standing in the middle of the road and breaking the legs of those who carry a tribute to the king - certainly such a man is deserving of death, for he prevents the many from bringing tribute to the king. Therefore let there be no such thing in Israel.
Pele Yoetz 62:69: It is forbidden to give a hand to transgressors. Included in this is one who says to the evil, "you are good," or who acknowledges falsehood and injustice, or who testifies falsely.
Pele Yoetz 62:70: It is forbidden to praise oneself with a false claim, or even with a true one. It is forbidden to tell of one's own righteous deeds and good works, as it is written, "let a stranger praise you, and not your own mouth" (Proverbs 27:2). And it is forbidden for a Torah scholar to show off his wisdom to the people out of arrogance, and even if others come and declare his righteousness, he shall be pained by it and humble himself - only it is permitted for a young Torah scholar to make himself known in a place where he is not known, in order to find lodging and the like, but he should not make words of Torah into a crown to adorn himself with, nor a spade to dig with. And it is forbidden to raise one's voice in prayers, weeping, and Torah reading out of arrogance, and especially in the Amidah prayer, of which they said (Berachot 24b): whoever makes his voice heard is among those of little faith, and whoever raises his voice is among the false prophets.
Pele Yoetz 62:71: Whoever disputes his teacher is as though he disputes the Shechinah (Sanhedrin 110a). Whoever complains against his teacher is as though he complains against the Shechinah. Whoever disgraces a Torah scholar with words is liable to excommunication (Yerushalmi Mo'ed Katan 3:1; Rambam, Talmud Torah 6:12). And to what extent is one called a disgracer? For example, one who says "these rabbis" [disrespectfully] (Sanhedrin 100a).
Pele Yoetz 62:72: Whoever honors himself through his fellow's disgrace has no share in the World to Come (Yerushalmi Chagigah 2:1), and he is not presumed to return in repentance, since it seems to him that he does not sin, and this is a severe sin (Rambam, Hilchot Teshuvah 3:4).
Pele Yoetz 62:73: There is an ancient ban against spreading a bad name about the dead.
Pele Yoetz 62:74: Whoever reveals a secret is as though he worships idols. And whatever one was not told to say, even though it was not explicitly told to him that it was a secret, falls under "he shall not say it" (Yoma 4b).
Pele Yoetz 62:75: Whoever stammers with his tongue in words of Torah, prayers, and blessings - of him Scripture says (Ezekiel 20:25): "and I also gave them statutes that were not good, and ordinances by which they could not live." And likewise one who reads a verse [of Torah] in the manner of song and melody - the Torah girds itself with sackcloth and says before the Holy One, blessed be He: Your children have made me like a musical instrument (Sanhedrin 101a). And it is possible that regarding Psalms there is no such concern, since its essence is song and hymns - but this applies specifically when done for the sake of Heaven, and not in the manner of idle occupation or in the manner of jest.
Pele Yoetz 62:76: It is forbidden to speak of matters that lead to evil rumination and arousal, God forbid. And the modest withdraw their hands from speaking even words of Torah regarding the details of the laws of husband and wife, and all the more so in the presence of the common people, for there is reason to fear that their reward be lost through their loss. And especially one who is unmarried - "go your way" we say to a Nazirite; "go around, go around, but do not approach the vineyard" (Shabbat 13a).
Pele Yoetz 62:77: Whoever asks his fellow to give him some utensil or object as a gift transgresses "you shall not covet." And if he gives it to him out of embarrassment, against his will and to his disadvantage, there is also an element of theft in it (Sefer Chasidim, 316).
Pele Yoetz 62:78: It is forbidden for a person to say "I have not sinned," and to seek pretexts to clear himself with vain and misleading claims - for it is written (Jeremiah 2:35): "behold, I shall enter into judgment with you, because you say, 'I have not sinned.'" And this was the difference between Saul and David: Saul sought to clear himself with claims, and therefore it did not succeed for him, but David immediately said "I have sinned," and Nathan the prophet answered him (II Samuel 12:13), "the LORD has also removed your sin." And even among people, whoever confesses is shown mercy - not so one who seeks pretexts and excuses; the heart knows whether it is crooked or straight, and words of truth are recognizable, and the listener's anger shall be kindled, for the latter sin is greater than the first, since he regards his fellow as though he eats straw, likened to beasts who do not understand the honesty of true words.
Pele Yoetz 62:79: It is forbidden to hurl words toward Heaven and complain against His attributes, blessed be He, as though, God forbid, He were unjust in judgment - rather, let him believe that "the Rock, His work is perfect."
Pele Yoetz 62:80: It is forbidden to hand over judgment against one's fellow [i.e. complain to Heaven about him], for his sins are thereby mentioned and he himself is punished first (Rosh Hashanah 16b) - rather, let him always say, "may his Master forgive whoever has caused me distress," and through this he shall be beloved above and cherished below.
Pele Yoetz 62:81: It is forbidden to contradict the words of one's father, mother, or teachers by saying "it is not so" - of this it is said (Psalms 1:4), "not so the wicked." And even to arbitrate and say "my father spoke well" or "my teacher and master speaks well" is forbidden [as it implies the possibility of disagreement]. And even one's fellow's words should not be contradicted if there is reason to fear it shall lead to division and hatred.
